subject: physics
title: Reducing unwanted energy transfers
key_idea: Unwanted energy transfers can be reduced. **Lubrication** reduces friction. **Thermal insulation** reduces the rate of energy transfer by conduction. Thicker wires with low resistance waste less energy. A building cools more slowly if its walls are thicker or have a lower thermal conductivity.

blocks.text: Wasted energy is dissipated by heating the surroundings. Three methods reduce it.

More input energy becomes useful output energy, so the efficiency increases.

blocks.text: Buildings lose energy to the cold outside. Thermal insulation reduces the rate at which they cool.

items.meaning: How easily a material transfers energy by conduction. The higher it is, the higher the rate of transfer.
A material with a low thermal conductivity, so energy passes through it slowly.
How quickly a building or object loses energy to the surroundings.

items: A wall with a lower thermal conductivity has a lower rate of energy transfer.
A thicker wall has a lower rate of energy transfer.
So a thicker wall, or one made of an insulator, makes the building cool more slowly.
Insulation means less energy is needed to heat the house.

blocks.text: Reducing heat loss from a building

items: Fit cavity wall insulation, or add cladding or extra insulation.
Use double glazed windows.
Use double thicknesses of material in the walls.
Close windows and doors properly, and fit draught excluders.
Paint the outside silver, reflective or white.
Plant trees around the building as a windbreak.
Higher thermal conductivity means a higher rate of energy transfer.
Thicker walls and lower thermal conductivity lower the rate of cooling.
Insulation reduces the energy needed to heat a building.

blocks.text: You can compare insulators by seeing how fast hot water cools. This method uses a beaker of hot water inside a box.

items.text: Put a beaker of hot water in a box made of the material, such as cardboard.
Change the thickness of the material, or use different materials.
Use the same volume and same starting temperature of water.
Record the temperature with a thermometer every two minutes, timed with a stopwatch.
Work out the rate of cooling as change in temperature divided by time. Repeat and find the mean.

items: If the temperature falls by 20 °C in a shorter time, the material has a higher thermal conductivity.
If it takes longer, the material is the better insulator.
Change one variable and control the volume and starting temperature of the water.
A shorter cooling time for the same temperature fall means a higher thermal conductivity.
Repeat the readings and calculate a mean.

checks.q: Explain how oil improves the efficiency of a bicycle.
checks.a: Oil reduces friction, so less thermal energy is transferred. More useful energy is available from the same input energy.

checks.q: Explain why the wires to a car battery are thicker than the wires to each device.
checks.a: Thicker wires have a lower resistance, so less thermal energy is transferred in the wires.

checks.q: How does the rate of cooling of a house change if its walls are thicker?
checks.a: The rate of cooling is lower, because the rate of energy transfer through the walls is lower.

worked_example.question:
Cavity wall insulation is installed in the wall of a house.

Explain how the wall reduces unwanted energy transfers.
answer_points: The wall has two / three layers (or the wall is thick)
Cavity wall insulation / brick / block has a low thermal conductivity
So less energy is transferred by conduction (or the rate of energy transfer is lower)
worked_example.tip: Any reference to convection or radiation is ignored.

worked_example.question:
Oil is applied to the wheel of a bicycle.

Explain how the oil improves the efficiency of the bicycle.
answer_points: Oil provides lubrication, which reduces friction (and the amount of thermal energy transferred)
Extra useful energy is available, or less input energy is required
Efficiency = useful energy transferred (by the bicycle) ÷ total energy supplied (to the bicycle)
worked_example.tip: Less energy is wasted. For the last two marks, less input energy for the same output, or more output for the same input, both score.

worked_example.question:
A crane's lifting equipment contains moving parts. A workman suggests adding oil to these moving parts.

Explain how this will affect the efficiency.
answer_points: Oil provides lubrication / is a lubricant
Reduces transfer to the thermal store / less energy is wasted / less energy transferred to the surroundings
worked_example.tip: Any two of these points score the 2 marks. Heat is allowed for thermal energy.

items: Good thermal conductors, such as metals, transfer energy quickly. Bad conductors (thermal insulators), such as wood, plastic and air, transfer it slowly.
To compare conductors: heat one end of rods of the same size but different materials, and time how long energy takes to reach the other end. The shortest time shows the best conductor.
A kitchen pan has a metal base, a good conductor, so energy passes quickly to the food. Its handle is plastic or wood, an insulator, so it stays cool.
A radiator heats a room by convection. Air next to it warms, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises. Cooler, denser air sinks to take its place, and a convection current forms.

worked_example.question:
The water in a swimming pool cools down at night.
A plastic cover is placed over the water.

Explain why the plastic cover reduces how much the water cools down at night.
answer_points: The cover traps a layer of air.
Trapped air is a poor conductor, or a good insulator.
Plastic is a poor conductor, or a good insulator.
There is less evaporation from the water surface.
worked_example.tip: Any four of the points score. Saying that the cover traps heat does not score.

items: Trapped air is a good insulator. It cannot circulate, so convection is reduced as well as conduction.
Covering a liquid reduces evaporation from its surface, so less energy is transferred away.
